paragraphs.en: "I didn't like the {ending},"I said to my favorite college {professor}.It was my {junior} year of undergraduate {study}, and I was doing an {independent} study on Victorian {literature}.I had {just} {finish} {read} The Mill on the Floss by George Eliot, and I was {heartbroken} by the ending.Prof.Gracie, with all his patience, asked me to {think} about it beyond whether I {like} it or not.He suggested I think about the {difference} between endings that I wanted for the {character} and endings that were right for the characters, endings that satisfied the story even if they didn't have a {traditionally} positive outcome.Of course, I would have {favor} a {different} ending for Tom and Maggie Tulliver, but the ending they got did make the most {sense} for them.
paragraphs.cn: 我对我最喜欢的大学<u>教授</u>说："我不喜欢这个<u>结局</u>。"那是我本科<u>三年级</u>的时候，我正在做一项关于维多利亚<u>文学</u>的<u>独立研究</u>。我<u>刚刚读完</u>乔治·艾略特的《弗洛斯河上的磨坊》，结局令我<u>心碎</u>。格雷西教授非常有耐心，让我不要仅从自己<u>喜欢</u>与否的角度出发，而要深入<u>思考</u>这个问题。他建议我思考一下，我想要的<u>人物</u>结局与适合这些人物的结局之间有什么<u>不同</u>，想想即使没有<u>传统意义上</u>的好结果，也能让故事完整自洽的结局。当然，我<u>更希望</u>汤姆和玛吉·塔利弗有个<u>不一样的</u>结局，但书中的结局对他们来说确实是最<u>合理</u>的。

paragraphs.en: This was an {aha} moment for me, and I never thought about endings the {same} way {again}.From then on, if I wanted to read an ending guaranteed to be happy, I'd {pick} up a {romance} {novel} .If I wanted an ending I couldn't {guess}, I'd pick up a {mystery}.For an ending where I {kind} of knew what was going to happen, I'd choose {historical} {fiction} .Choosing what to read {became} easier.
paragraphs.cn: 那一刻，我<u>恍然大悟</u>，之后<u>再</u>也没有以<u>同样的</u>方式看待过结局。从那以后，如果我想读一个肯定会幸福的结局，我就会<u>选择</u><u>爱情小说</u>。如果我想读一个无法<u>预测</u>的结局，那我会选一本<u>悬疑小说</u>。如果是想读一个我<u>大致</u>知道会发生什么的结局，我会选择<u>历史小说</u>。选择阅读内容<u>变得</u>更容易了。

paragraphs.en: But {write} endings—that's {hard}.It's hard for {writer} {because} endings {carry} so much {weight} with readers.You have to {balance} {create} an ending that's {unpredictable}, yet doesn't seem to come from {nowhere}, one that fits what's right for the characters.
paragraphs.cn: 但是，要<u>写</u>出结局——那可是很<u>难的</u>。对<u>作家</u>来说很不容易，<u>因为</u>结局对读者来说<u>承载</u>了很重的<u>分量</u>。你必须做到<u>平衡</u>，<u>创作出</u>一个既<u>出人意料</u>又非<u>无</u>中生有的结局，一个符合人物设定的结局。

paragraphs.en: That's why this {issue} of Writers Digest aims to help you {figure} out how to write the best ending for whatever kind of writing you're doing.If it's short stories, Peter Mountford {break} down six techniques you can try to see which one helps you {stick} the {landing}.Elizabeth Sims analyzes the final chapters of five {great} novels to see what key points they include and how you can {adapt} them for your work.
paragraphs.cn: 这就是为什么本<u>期</u>《作家文摘》旨在帮助你<u>弄清楚</u>，无论你正在进行何种类型的写作，该如何写出最好的结局。如果是短篇小说，彼得·蒙福德为你<u>分解</u>出了六种技巧，你可以尝试看看哪一种能帮助你<u>顺利完成</u>写作。伊丽莎白·西姆斯分析了五部<u>优秀小说</u>的最终章，阐述了它们包含的关键点以及你如何将这些关键点<u>应用</u>到自己的作品中。

paragraphs.en: This issue won't tell you what your ending should be—that's {up} to you and the story you're telling—but it might {provide} what you need to get there.
paragraphs.cn: 本期内容不会告诉你结局应该是什么——这<u>取决于</u>你和你所讲述的故事——但它可能会为你<u>提供</u>通往那个结局所需要的东西。
